meta.title: oscp shell-script — bash you can copy into a file
meta.note: Snippets belong in a .sh file. Type a line number to copy one line, or N-M for a block. Adapt names, paths, and commands before you run them. This page does not execute the snippets.
meta.flow: oscp shell-script  →  pick a section (Tab lists them)  →  copy a line or a range

sections.name: Shebang, comments, and the first script
sections.goal: A script is a file of commands. The first line names the interpreter. The rest runs top to bottom.
sections.why: #!/usr/bin/env bash asks PATH for bash, so the same file works when bash is /bin/bash or /usr/local/bin/bash. A # line is a comment: the interpreter skips it. chmod +x lets you run ./name.sh.
sections.gotcha: A shebang only works as line 1, with no BOM and no spaces before #!. Typing commands in an interactive shell is not a script: aliases and history do not apply inside the file.
steps: choose the interpreter — must be line 1
# This script prints a short greeting.
send a message to standard error
make the file executable, then run it
a complete first script — save as hello.sh

rows: a file the interpreter reads; not the live prompt
line 1 names bash via env, not a hardcoded path
from # to end of line; use it to say why, not what
needed for ./script.sh; bash script.sh also runs it
the script's own name, useful in Usage: lines

sections.name: Strict mode, PATH, umask, and required commands
sections.goal: Fail early, keep PATH predictable, and refuse to run when a needed tool is missing.
sections.why: set -euo pipefail is a default, not magic. set -e exits on a failing command; a command in an if test is exempt. set -u treats unset variables as errors. pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails. umask 077 makes new files private to you.
sections.gotcha: Do not paste set -e into a script you have not walked through. A grep that finds nothing returns 1 and will abort the script. Test the failure path. (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] >= 4 )) needs Bash 4; macOS /bin/bash is still 3.2 unless you installed a newer bash.
steps: strict-mode defaults; understand set -e before relying on it
restrictive default permission mask for new files
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is required" >&2; exit 127; }

rows: exit when a command fails (not when it is the if test)
exit when expanding an unset variable
a pipeline fails if any stage fails
PATH lookup; exit 127 is the usual missing-tool status

sections.name: Assignment, export, capture, and status
sections.goal: Names hold text. There is no space around =. Quote expansions. $? is the last command's status, and it changes on the next command.
sections.why: A variable is local to this shell until you export it. output=$(cmd) runs cmd in a subshell and stores stdout. APP_ENV=test cmd sets the value only for that one command.
sections.gotcha: var = value is a command named var, not an assignment. echo $status after another command is already the later status. Capture $? immediately. $(cmd) strips trailing newlines.
steps:
if output=$(some_command); then
  printf '%s\n' "$output"
else
  echo "Command failed" >&2
fi
read a command's exit status immediately

sections.name: Quotes, --, and ${} expansions
sections.goal: Quote first. "$var" keeps spaces and glob characters. 'literal' does not expand. ${var} is the same name with a boundary. ${var:-default} fills in a missing or empty value.
sections.why: Word splitting and globbing happen after unquoted expansion. cp -- "$src" "$dst" so a name that starts with - is a filename, not a flag. ${path##*/} is the basename; ${file%.*} drops the shortest suffix.
sections.gotcha: [[ -v name ]] is true when the name is set, even to empty. ${1:-guest} is guest when $1 is unset or empty. ${CONFIG-default} (one dash) only substitutes when unset. Always quote: rm -- "$filename".
steps: quote variables to preserve spaces and globs
-- so a name beginning with - is a filename
single quotes: literal text, no expansion
require a variable to be set and nonempty
check whether a variable is set
if [[ -v config ]]; then echo "config is set"; fi
if [[ -n "${value:-}" ]]; then echo "Has a value"; fi

rows: expand, keep spaces, do not glob

sections.name: Tests, if / elif / else, case, and regex
sections.goal: [[ ]] is the Bash test. if runs a branch. case picks among several fixed words. (( )) is integer arithmetic.
sections.why: [[ -f "$path" ]] is a regular file. [[ "$a" == "$b" ]] is string equality. [[ "$f" == *.log ]] is a pattern, not a regex. [[ "$user" =~ ^[[:alnum:]_-]+$ ]] is a regex; groups land in BASH_REMATCH.
sections.gotcha: [ is test(1) and needs more quoting. Use [[ in bash scripts. = inside [[ is string compare; (( count >= 10 )) is integer. A missing fi or esac is a parse error. case patterns are glob, not regex.
steps:
if [[ "$mode" == "fast" ]]; then
  echo "Fast mode"
elif [[ "$mode" == "safe" ]]; then
  echo "Safe mode"
else
  echo "Default mode"
fi
if (( count >= 10 )); then echo "At least ten"; fi

if ! some_command; then
  echo "Could not complete operation" >&2
  exit 1
fi
stop a script when input is missing

rows: string equal / not equal (quote both sides)

sections.name: for, while, read, break, continue, select
sections.goal: A loop repeats. for walks a list. while repeats a test. read walks a file one line at a time. break leaves; continue skips to the next pass.
sections.why: for x in "$@" keeps each argument whole. {1..5} is a brace range, expanded before the loop. while IFS= read -r line keeps spaces and backslashes. The || [[ -n "$line" ]] clause keeps a file that has no final newline.
sections.gotcha: for f in $(ls) splits names on spaces — do not parse ls. A pipeline while read runs in a subshell, so assignments inside it are lost; use < file or process substitution. select is a menu, not a hidden loop over files.
steps: for color in red green blue; do printf '%s\n' "$color"; done
for number in {1..5}; do echo "$number"; done
loop while a condition is true
read lines from a file without trimming spaces

while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
  printf '%s\n' "$line"
done < "$input_file"
select for a simple interactive menu

select choice in Start Stop Quit; do
  case "$choice" in Start) echo "Starting";; Stop) echo "Stopping";; Quit) break;; esac
done
group commands in the current shell

sections.name: Positional arguments, $@, shift, and getopts
sections.goal: $1 is the first argument. $# is how many. "$@" is every argument, each kept whole. getopts parses short options.
sections.why: Always iterate with for arg in "$@" — not $*. shift drops $1 and renumbers the rest. getopts ':f:vn' means f takes a value; v and n are flags. After the loop, shift "$((OPTIND - 1))" leaves only operands.
sections.gotcha: Unquoted $@ splits. Missing operands should exit 2 with a Usage line. getopts does not parse --long options; use a case on $1 for those, or a dedicated parser.
steps: for arg in "$@"; do printf 'Argument: %s\n' "$arg"; done

rows: value of the option getopts just saw

sections.name: Define, local, return, main, and source
sections.goal: A function is a named block. local keeps names inside it. return leaves the function; exit leaves the script. source loads another file into this shell.
sections.why: name() { … } is the usual form. stdout is how a function returns text: today=$(get_date). Check [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]] so library files can be sourced without running main.
sections.gotcha: A function sees the caller's variables unless you local them. return 1 is a status, not printed output. source ./lib.sh runs in this shell — a cd inside it changes the caller's directory unless you isolate it.
steps: printf -v assigns formatted output without a subshell
check whether a function is defined
run main only when the file is executed, not sourced
source a library next to this script
nameref to modify a caller's variable (Bash 4.3+)

set_value() { local -n target=$1; target=$2; }
set_value result "done"

sections.name: Indexed arrays, associative arrays, mapfile, and input
sections.goal: An array is a list. "${arr[@]}" expands each element quoted. declare -A is a map from keys to values (Bash 4+). mapfile reads lines into an array. read pulls fields into names.
sections.why: servers+=("x") appends. ${#servers[@]} is the count. "${!servers[@]}" is the indices. IFS=, read -r a b c <<< "$record" splits one line. A quoted here-document <<'EOF' does not expand $var.
sections.gotcha: macOS /bin/bash 3.2 has no declare -A. Quote "${arr[@]}"; unquoted ${arr[@]} splits again. mapfile drops the last incomplete line unless you handle it. read -s still writes the prompt to stderr; printf '\n' after it so the cursor moves.
steps:
for index in "${!servers[@]}"; do
  printf '%s=%s\n' "$index" "${servers[index]}"
done
for key in "${!ports[@]}"; do printf '%s=%s\n' "$key" "${ports[$key]}"; done
load file lines into an array
read a delimited record into variables
custom field separator for one read

cat <<'EOF'
Literal $text is not expanded here.
EOF
here-string for one line of input
if IFS= read -r -t 10 answer; then echo "Received input"; fi

while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
  process_line "$line"
done < "$input_file"

sections.name: Paths, mkdir, mktemp, trap, find, and glob
sections.goal: Quote paths. mkdir -p creates parents. mktemp makes a unique name. trap runs cleanup on EXIT. find walks a tree without parsing ls. A quoted glob is just characters; an unquoted glob is a list of names.
sections.why: mktemp and a trap to rm -f is the safe temp-file pair. find -print0 / read -d '' / xargs -0 keep names with spaces and newlines. script_dir=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd -P) is this file's directory.
sections.gotcha: cd in the current shell changes the caller's directory forever; use a subshell ( cd -- dir && cmd ) unless you mean it. Do not parse ls. nullglob makes unmatched *.log expand to nothing instead of the literal *.log.
steps:
while IFS= read -r -d '' path; do
  printf '%s\n' "$path"
done < <(find "$root" -type f -print0)
glob for files in one directory — do not parse ls

for path in "$directory"/*; do
  [[ -e "$path" ]] || continue
  printf '%s\n' "$path"
done
nullglob so unmatched patterns expand to nothing

shopt -s globstar nullglob
for path in "$root"/**/*.conf; do printf '%s\n' "$path"; done
do not change the caller's working directory
save and restore PWD in the same shell

sections.name: Redirection, pipelines, jobs, locks, and exec
sections.goal: > writes a file. >> appends. 2> is stderr. | is a pipeline. & is background. wait collects the status. exec replaces this process.
sections.why: cmd > f 2>&1 sends both streams to f. set -o pipefail so a failing producer is not hidden by a successful consumer. PIPESTATUS is the status of each stage, and it is overwritten by the next command — copy it immediately. timeout and flock exist on GNU coreutils; they may be missing on a stock macOS.
sections.gotcha: cmd > f 2>&1 is not the same as cmd 2>&1 > f. Background jobs keep running if you forget wait. mkdir as a lock is not atomic on every filesystem; prefer flock where it exists. exec cmd never returns to the script.
steps: replace a file with command output
if wait "$pid"; then echo "Completed"; else echo "Failed" >&2; fi

job_a & pid_a=$!
job_b & pid_b=$!
wait "$pid_a"
wait "$pid_b"
lock directory as a simple alternative

for attempt in {1..3}; do
  some_command && break
  (( attempt == 3 )) && exit 1
  sleep "$attempt"
done

delay=1
for attempt in {1..5}; do
  some_command && break
  (( attempt == 5 )) && exit 1
  sleep "$delay"
  (( delay = delay < 16 ? delay * 2 : 16 ))
done
replace this process with the final command

rows: stdout of cmd1 is stdin of cmd2
block; status is that job's status

sections.name: No eval, validate input, hide secrets, check the script
sections.goal: Keep untrusted text out of command names. Put arguments in an array. Validate names before they become paths. Do not print tokens. Run shellcheck.
sections.why: eval concatenates a string and runs it as code — a space or a quote in user input becomes syntax. args=(--name "$user_input"); cmd "${args[@]}" keeps the value as one argument. LC_ALL=C makes sort and [a-z] ranges predictable.
sections.gotcha: A regex that allows / or .. still lets a path walk up the tree. ${API_TOKEN:+[set]} prints [set] when the token is nonempty and prints nothing when it is empty — never the token. bash -n parses; it does not run. shellcheck is the review.
steps: avoid eval; keep arguments in an array
validate untrusted input before paths or commands
locale for predictable sorting and ranges
parse and lint; use bash for bash-only features
